newsitem.title: INDIA: India power shortage due to red tape-power sector.
newsitem.headline: India power shortage due to red tape-power sector.

text.p: Senior power sector officials on Saturday blamed complex and inefficient Indian bureaucratic procedures for an acute power shortage that appears to be thwarting industrial growth.

"Contrary to the popular perception that a lack of funds is constraining implementation of power projects in India, my submission is the case is not so," Reliance Power Ltd chairman D.V. Kapur told an international business seminar in New Delhi.

"Unlike major liberalised policy measures taken in (other) sectors, there really has been no significant attempt to demolish the various regulatory shackles and complex procedural hurdles in infrastructure management," Kapur said.
India in 1991 launched a market-oriented economic reforms programme, dismantling tariff barriers and inviting private and foreign investment into its economy.

The government says it needs investments worth $79 billion to ease acute power shortages. It could add only 14,799 megawatts in power generation capacity during the first four years of its Eighth Five-Year Plan (1992-97), which had envisaged an addition of 30,858 megawatts in the five years.
Kapur said demand for electricity was growing at about 12 percent annually but power generation capacity over the past 10 months had expanded by as little as three percent.

U.S. energy giant Enron Development Corp's chief executive Rebecca Mark said even competitive private bidding for power projects -- for decades a state monopoly -- had not introduced transparency or efficiency in the sector.
"We bid and we won, but we were still under attack. We negotiated and we won, but we were still under attack. How does it work? We haven't a clue," Mark said.

Enron was forced to renegotiate a contract for a $2.3 billion power plant in the western Indian state of Maharashtra last year after the state government said the 2,450-megawatt plant's project costs and tariffs were too high.

Mark said: "The lack of investment is evidence that we simply don't have the process right. It's not a lack of money -- it's that the process doesn't allow us to invest that money in a way that is time-effective and cost-effective."
"(And) This government does not have the sense of urgency and the crisis mentality needed to solve the problem," she said.

Hopewell Holdings Ltd managing director Gordon Wu said India consumed only 350 kilowatt hours of power every year, compared with the United States' annual per capita consumption 11,000 and Japan's 7,000.
"You keep your democracy but drop your socialism," he said. "Cut the red tape."
